title: Build a DMZ for Your IIS Help Desk
description: Build a safe front door for a practice help desk. Keep IIS private, let approved web requests through, and check that other connections stay blocked.
baseline: Windows 10 host / Workstation Pro · OPNsense Community · AlmaLinux 9 / NGINX · Windows Server 2019 / IIS · isolated practice only
prerequisite: Start with the linked VMware, Windows Server and IIS lessons. You also need the AlmaLinux installation and terminal lessons. We will use four new practice VMs: a firewall, a gateway, an IIS server and a pretend visitor. Leave DC01, DC02 and your existing APP01 alone.
supplies: A patched host with Workstation Pro, approximately 24–32 GB RAM and 200 GB free disk space.
Verified OPNsense/AlmaLinux media and valid Windows Server 2019 media/evaluation entitlement.
Access to the Windows host and each VM console; a private password manager and backup location.
No Azure subscription, home-router port forwarding or public DNS change is needed.

sources.title: OPNsense firewall rules and processing order
NGINX upstream HTTPS and certificate verification
Azure Application Gateway and firewall architecture

lessons.title: Meet the DMZ: Your Application’s Front Door
lessons.description: Learn where the help desk, gateway and firewall belong before changing any settings.
lessons.what: Learn where the help desk, gateway and firewall belong before changing any settings.
lessons.why: Imagine an office reception area. Visitors speak to the receptionist, not directly to everyone inside. Our DMZ is that reception area. A gateway there receives web requests and passes only the approved requests to IIS in a separate private network. DMZ stands for demilitarized zone: a separate network between visitors and the private servers.
needs: Complete the Windows/VMware installation and IIS basics first. The public course link for those classes stays in the Windows pathway.
Use a supported, patched Windows host with Workstation Pro. A Windows 10 host needs applicable security updates/ESU; keep this lab isolated.
Plan around 24–32 GB host RAM and 200 GB free disk space for this four-VM exercise; you can shut down unrelated practice VMs. No Azure subscription is required.
bestPractices: Get the small test page working before adding a full help desk. This makes it easier to tell an application problem from a network problem.

For a real help desk, install and test it on a private IIS application server first. Point the gateway at its approved HTTPS binding; keep the database private and allow only the specific application-to-database connection it needs. Test sign-in, links, attachments and sign-out before any public launch. Use the IIS help desk class for the application install; copying website files alone is not a complete migration.
commonMistakes: Putting a reverse proxy in front does not make it a WAF or a fully production-ready deployment.

troubleshooting.problem: My interface names or addresses differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and compare the MAC address and VMnet assignment on each adapter. Use the VMware console to recover access; do not guess which interface is private.

lessons.pass: A saved diagram, resource budget and non-overlapping address inventory are complete.
lessons.exercise: Explain the request route to someone who has never configured a firewall. Point out why a reverse proxy is not a WAF or a replacement for patching.

quiz.question: What belongs in the DMZ for this design?
options: The reverse proxy; IIS stays private
quiz.explanation: The DMZ proxy receives visitor requests and can reach only the explicitly allowed private web endpoint.

steps.title: Trace a visitor’s request
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notebook
actions: Open My lab notebook above. In “What application am I protecting?”, type practice help desk. Click Save notes.
Picture someone opening your help desk in a browser. They ask for a page; they do not need access to your server’s desktop or database.
Write this route in your notes: TEST01 visitor → FW01 firewall → PROXY01 gateway in the DMZ → IIS-DMZ01 private website.
The DMZ contains PROXY01 only. IIS-DMZ01 stays on its own private application network. DC01, DC02 and SQL stay out of the DMZ.
Use app-dmz.cloudseam.tech as the visitor’s practice website name. This does not create a public DNS record or change cloudseam.tech.

In this class we build a harmless test page, not another osTicket installation. A real help desk would use the same approved web route, with its own application and database connections reviewed separately.

breakdown.meaning: A separate network for the public-facing entry point. Its firewall rules limit what that entry point can reach.
A server that receives a web request and makes an approved request to your private web server.

steps.expected: Your diagram shows the visitor reaching only the gateway. The gateway can request a page from private IIS. AD and SQL stay outside the DMZ.

screenshot.title: Trace a visitor’s request
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. Your diagram separates visitor, DMZ, private application and private AD/management zones with one approved HTTPS route.

steps.title: Choose your practice setup
steps.where: Your Windows host · lab notebook
actions: Use VMware Workstation Pro for this first build. The firewall is OPNsense, the gateway runs AlmaLinux with NGINX, and the private website runs Windows Server 2019 with IIS.
Use the installation lessons linked above if you have not installed those operating systems yet. Come back here after the new VMs are ready.
Create a new IIS-DMZ01. Do not replace APP01 or copy a domain controller to make it.
Use another new VM, TEST01, to pretend to be the visitor. Do not use your Windows host for this test: it already has access to the private lab network.
Do not add a home-router port forward, bridge, tunnel or public DNS record. We are practicing the design inside VMware.
Leave Azure for the final planning lesson. A managed Azure web gateway has ongoing charges; we are not promising an always-on $25 cloud setup.

breakdown.meaning: The same request-boundary concepts can be practiced without running a paid cloud gateway or opening your home router.

steps.expected: Your plan uses four new VMs inside VMware. No Internet publishing or Azure deployment is planned yet.

screenshot.title: Choose your practice setup
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The plan is local and isolated. Azure is a later design comparison, not a resource deployment.

steps.title: Write down the four networks
steps.where: Windows host · VMware Virtual Network Editor and lab notebook
actions: In My lab notebook, click Show my whole lab plan. Write these four network ranges before opening VMware settings.
Existing AD and management: VMnet2, 10.50.0.0/24. Keep DC01 at 10.50.0.10 and DC02 at 10.50.0.11.
DMZ: VMnet3, 10.60.0.0/24. PROXY01 will use 10.60.0.10 and the firewall will use 10.60.0.1.
Pretend outside visitor: VMnet4, 10.70.0.0/24. TEST01 will use 10.70.0.10 and the firewall will use 10.70.0.1.
Private application: VMnet5, 10.80.0.0/24. IIS-DMZ01 will use 10.80.0.40 and the firewall will use 10.80.0.1.
On VMnet2, reserve 10.50.0.1 for the firewall and 10.50.0.254 for the Windows host’s management adapter. Check that neither address is already used.

The /24 means a mask of 255.255.255.0. If any planned range overlaps your home network, VPN or another lab, stop and resolve that before building. Leave your existing servers’ gateways and DNS unchanged.
Click Save notes. The new IIS server stays in a workgroup; we are not joining it to Active Directory.

breakdown.meaning: A subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. Addresses in each lab subnet share the first three numbers.
IIS uses 10.80.0.0/24, so reaching AD on 10.50.0.0/24 must cross the firewall.

steps.expected: Your notebook lists four different network ranges and unique addresses. DC01 and DC02 keep their existing settings.

screenshot.title: Write down the four networks
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. Your inventory shows unique addresses, unchanged DC01/DC02 and no overlapping subnets.

lessons.title: Build the Four Practice Networks
lessons.description: Create the four private VMware networks that separate your visitor, gateway, IIS server and existing domain controllers.
lessons.what: Create the four private VMware networks that separate your visitor, gateway, IIS server and existing domain controllers.
lessons.why: A network is a group of computers that can talk directly. Separate networks let our firewall decide which groups may talk to each other. We need four because the private application must also stay separate from Active Directory.
needs: Use the address plan from the previous lesson.
Download verified supported OPNsense amd64 DVD ISO, AlmaLinux 9 ISO and licensed/evaluation Windows Server 2019 media from the publishers. Use evaluation software only within its terms.
bestPractices: Verify both the virtual-switch settings and every guest’s adapter list.
commonMistakes: Changing the physical adapter instead of the named VMware management adapter.

troubleshooting.problem: My interface names or addresses differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and compare the MAC address and VMnet assignment on each adapter. Use the VMware console to recover access; do not guess which interface is private.

lessons.pass: The saved VMnet settings and NIC/MAC inventory match the diagram; original domain controllers remain unchanged.
lessons.exercise: Reopen every guest’s settings and audit the adapters without looking at your earlier checklist.

quiz.question: Which adapter creates a bypass around the lab firewall?
options: An extra NAT or bridged NIC on a protected server
quiz.explanation: A second network connection can provide a path that never crosses FW01.

steps.title: Prepare the four new VMs
steps.where: Windows host · Workstation Pro; Linux guest consoles during preparation
actions: Create a new FW01 VM: 2 processors, 4 GB memory and a 40 GB virtual disk. Attach the OPNsense DVD ISO. Choose the supported FreeBSD 64-bit guest type; follow OPNsense’s guide for Secure Boot.
Use the linked Windows installation lesson to create IIS-DMZ01: Server 2019 Standard Desktop Experience, 4 GB memory and 60 GB disk.
Use the linked AlmaLinux installation lesson to create PROXY01: Minimal Install, 2 GB memory and 30 GB disk. Create TEST01 with Workstation/GNOME, 3 GB memory and 30 GB disk.
For package downloads only, give PROXY01 and TEST01 one NAT adapter on VMnet8. We will remove this connection before the isolation tests.
On PROXY01, open its console and run the command block below. It updates AlmaLinux and installs the gateway tools.
On TEST01, open Terminal. Run sudo dnf upgrade --refresh -y. When it finishes, run sudo dnf install -y curl openssl open-vm-tools fuse3. Then run sudo systemctl enable --now vmtoolsd.
Install VMware Tools in the Windows guest and apply its available updates. These tools will let us temporarily copy public certificate files through a shared folder.
Shut down IIS-DMZ01, PROXY01 and TEST01. Keep them off while changing their adapters.
steps.command:
sudo dnf upgrade --refresh -y
sudo dnf install -y nginx openssl curl tcpdump open-vm-tools fuse3 policycoreutils-python-utils
sudo systemctl enable --now vmtoolsd

breakdown.meaning: Install packages while temporary NAT access exists. The final networks deliberately have no Internet upstream.

steps.expected: Your new VMs are installed, updated and shut down, ready for the network changes.

screenshot.title: Prepare the four new VMs
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The guests are prepared, powered off and ready to be attached to isolated networks.

steps.title: Create the VMware networks
steps.where: Windows host · VMware Workstation Pro → Edit → Virtual Network Editor
actions: In VMware Workstation Pro on your Windows host, click Edit → Virtual Network Editor.
Click Change Settings. Approve the Windows administrator prompt.

Select VMnet2. Confirm Host-only, Subnet IP 10.50.0.0 and Subnet mask 255.255.255.0. Leave its existing host adapter enabled. Clear the local DHCP checkbox. If these settings already match, leave them alone.
Click Add Network, select VMnet3 and click OK. Select Host-only. Enter Subnet IP 10.60.0.0 and mask 255.255.255.0.
For VMnet3, clear both “Connect a host virtual adapter” and “Use local DHCP service”. We will assign our own addresses.
Add VMnet4 the same way, using Subnet IP 10.70.0.0. Add VMnet5 using 10.80.0.0. Both use mask 255.255.255.0; clear the host adapter and DHCP checkboxes on both.
Click Apply, then OK. Reopen the editor and check all four networks. None should be Bridged or NAT.

breakdown.meaning: A VMware virtual switch separate from the physical LAN; traffic crosses to another lab network only through the configured firewall.
Every lab address is assigned deliberately instead of being leased by VMware.

steps.expected: VMnet2, VMnet3, VMnet4 and VMnet5 show Host-only with DHCP off. Only VMnet2 has a host management adapter.

screenshot.title: Create the VMware networks
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. VMnet2/3/4/5 are isolated host-only /24 networks with DHCP off. Only VMnet2 has the intended host management adapter.

steps.title: Set the Windows host’s management address
steps.where: Windows 10 host · Run → ncpa.cpl
actions: On the Windows host, press Windows+R. Type ncpa.cpl and press Enter. This opens Network Connections.
Find VMware Network Adapter VMnet2. Do not choose Wi-Fi or your physical Ethernet adapter.
Right-click VMnet2 → Properties. Select Internet Protocol Version 4 → Properties. Write down its old settings before changing them.
Select Use the following IP address. Enter 10.50.0.254 for IP address and 255.255.255.0 for Subnet mask.
Leave Default gateway and DNS blank on this VMware management adapter. Click OK, then OK again.
Open PowerShell on the Windows host. Run ipconfig and find the VMnet2 section. Check that it shows 10.50.0.254. Your physical network adapter should still have its original settings.
Do not enable Internet Connection Sharing or Network Bridge. The host adapter is for managing the firewall, not for pretending to be an outside visitor.

breakdown.meaning: The host needs a private management address that does not conflict with FW01 at .1. This does not change your physical Wi-Fi or Ethernet settings.

steps.expected: The Windows host’s VMnet2 adapter shows 10.50.0.254. Its physical Wi-Fi or Ethernet settings have not changed.

screenshot.title: Set the Windows host’s management address
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The host VMnet2 adapter is 10.50.0.254 and does not conflict with the future FW01 .1 address.

steps.title: Connect each VM to the right network
steps.where: Workstation Pro · each powered-off VM → Settings → Network Adapter
actions: With FW01 powered off, right-click it → Settings. Open its first Network Adapter. Choose Custom → VMnet4. This is OUTSIDE.
Add three more Network Adapters with Add → Network Adapter. Set adapter 2 to Custom VMnet2, adapter 3 to Custom VMnet3 and adapter 4 to Custom VMnet5.
For each FW01 adapter, open Advanced and copy its MAC address into My lab notebook. Label each one OUTSIDE, PRIVATE/AD, DMZ or APP_PRIVATE. A MAC address identifies the adapter when OPNsense starts.
Open IIS-DMZ01 Settings. Give it just one adapter: Custom VMnet5.
Give PROXY01 just one adapter: Custom VMnet3. Give TEST01 just one adapter: Custom VMnet4.
Remove or disconnect the temporary VMnet8 adapters and any extra adapters. No final VM should have a bridged adapter.
Check Connected and Connect at power on for the intended adapters. Save, reopen Settings and compare with your notebook. Only FW01 should have four adapters.

breakdown.meaning: The adapter identifier used to match an operating-system interface to the correct VMware virtual cable.
Prevents an extra NAT or bridged connection from bypassing FW01.

steps.expected: FW01 has four adapters with recorded MAC addresses. Each other new VM has just one adapter on the correct VMnet.

screenshot.title: Connect each VM to the right network
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The saved four-zone MAC/NIC inventory has four FW01 adapters and one adapter on each server/client.

lessons.title: Set Up the Firewall and Its Rules
lessons.description: Install OPNsense, name its four connections and allow the gateway to reach only the IIS web service.
lessons.what: Install OPNsense, name its four connections and allow the gateway to reach only the IIS web service.
lessons.why: The firewall acts like a security guard. A rule tells it who may connect, where they may go and which service they may use. We will write specific rules instead of giving every server access to everything.
needs: FW01, the four custom VMnets and the MAC inventory are ready.
Use the VMware console for recovery. Keep a private password manager available; screenshots never show your real password.
bestPractices: Keep console recovery and a private configuration backup ready before removing broad management access.
commonMistakes: Assuming an existing browser connection proves the new narrow management rule works.

troubleshooting.problem: The firewall page disappeared after the management rule change.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the VMware console open. Check the LAN MAC/IP and restore the private backup if needed. Recheck the explicit ADMIN_HOST-to-LAN-443 rule before attempting lockdown again.

lessons.pass: A private backup and screenshots show the interface mapping, administrator rule and narrow DMZ HTTPS rule in the correct order.
lessons.exercise: Explain why the reply from IIS does not need a separate broad PRIVATE-to-DMZ allow rule.

quiz.question: Where is the proxy-to-IIS rule placed?
options: The DMZ interface where that connection enters FW01
quiz.explanation: Interface rules normally evaluate new traffic entering that interface. Existing allowed connection states carry the response back.

steps.title: Install the firewall on FW01
steps.where: FW01 VMware console · OPNsense installer
actions: Power on FW01 using the OPNsense DVD ISO. At the login prompt, use installer with the initial password opnsense. These defaults are only for installation.
Choose your keyboard layout. Choose Install (UFS), if offered for this simple one-disk VM.
Select FW01’s new 40 GB virtual disk. Check the disk carefully before confirming an erase. Never select a physical Windows host disk.
Set your own strong root password when asked. Keep it in your password manager, not in the notebook.
Finish installation, disconnect the ISO in VMware and restart FW01 from its virtual disk.
Sign in as root with your new password. Select Assign interfaces. Answer no to creating VLANs for this lab.
Match the displayed MAC addresses with your notebook: WAN = VMnet4, LAN = VMnet2, OPT1 = VMnet3 and OPT2 = VMnet5. Do not guess from names such as em0.

breakdown.meaning: The installer account starts installation. Your chosen root password is for the installed firewall; do not keep the published installer default.

steps.expected: FW01 starts from its virtual disk. Its four network adapters match the MAC addresses in your notes.

screenshot.title: Install the firewall on FW01
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. FW01 boots from disk with WAN, LAN, OPT1 and OPT2 mapped to the correct recorded MACs.

steps.title: Give the firewall its four addresses
steps.where: FW01 console · Set interface IP address
actions: At the FW01 console menu, select Set interface IP address, then LAN.
Choose a static IPv4 address. Enter 10.50.0.1 and prefix 24. Leave the upstream gateway empty. Say no to DHCP and IPv6 setup for this lab. Keep HTTPS for administration.
Repeat for WAN: address 10.70.0.1, prefix 24, no upstream gateway, no DHCP and no IPv6. This is our pretend outside network, not an Internet connection.
Repeat for OPT1 with 10.60.0.1/24 and OPT2 with 10.80.0.1/24. Again, no upstream gateway, DHCP or IPv6.
Compare the four addresses on the console with your notebook. Correct any mix-up before continuing.

On your Windows host, open a browser and enter https://10.50.0.1. Check that you are reaching your own isolated firewall. Verify its initial self-signed certificate before accepting a lab-only browser exception. Real deployments need a trusted management certificate.

breakdown.meaning: The isolated outside segment has no real Internet router. Internal interface gateways are not configured as upstream WAN gateways.

steps.expected: Your Windows host opens the firewall at 10.50.0.1. All four firewall addresses match your plan.

screenshot.title: Give the firewall its four addresses
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The host reaches FW01 on 10.50.0.1 and all four interface addresses match the diagram.

steps.title: Name the firewall connections
steps.where: Windows host browser · FW01 Interfaces
actions: Sign in to the firewall web page as root with your own password. Write the installed OPNsense version in your notebook.
Open System → Settings → General. Set Hostname to fw01 and Domain to cloudseam.tech. Save. This names the firewall; it does not join a Windows domain or change public DNS.
Open Interfaces → OPT1. Check Enable, set Description to DMZ and confirm 10.60.0.1/24. Save and apply.
Open Interfaces → OPT2. Check Enable, set Description to APP_PRIVATE and confirm 10.80.0.1/24. Save and apply. LAN remains private management; WAN is our pretend OUTSIDE.
Open Interfaces → WAN. For this isolated practice network only, clear Block private networks. Also clear Block bogon networks if it blocks this lab range. Save and apply.
Why? Our pretend outside address starts with 10, which is a private address. On a real Internet-facing WAN, keep these protections unless your documented design requires otherwise.
Open System → Settings → Administration. If your release offers Listen Interfaces, choose PRIVATE/LAN only. Keep the VMware console open so you can recover if browser access fails.

breakdown.meaning: A real WAN often rejects private source addresses. This lab’s simulated outside uses 10.70.0.0/24, so that lab interface needs a deliberate exception.

steps.expected: DMZ and APP_PRIVATE are enabled and named correctly. Firewall administration listens only on the private management connection.

screenshot.title: Name the firewall connections
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The DMZ is enabled, the test outside interface accepts the planned private lab addresses, and management is confined to PRIVATE.

steps.title: Keep your administrator access working
steps.where: Windows host browser · Firewall → Aliases, then Rules [new] / interface rules
actions: Open Firewall → Aliases. Add Host aliases named ADMIN_HOST (10.50.0.254), DMZ_PROXY (10.60.0.10), PRIVATE_IIS (10.80.0.40) and LAB_VISITOR (10.70.0.10). Save and apply. An alias is a short label for an address.
Open Firewall → Rules → LAN. Add a Pass rule: IPv4, TCP, source ADMIN_HOST, destination LAN address, destination port HTTPS (443).
Check Log. Enter description ADMIN_TO_FW_HTTPS. Save, move it above broad rules and apply. This is your named doorway into firewall settings.
Before removing anything, export a private firewall backup and confirm that your root login works in the VMware console. Keep the console open.
Recheck your new rule. Then disable the default LAN-to-any IPv4 and IPv6 rules and the automatic anti-lockout rule. Apply. The new explicit rule must now be the management doorway.

Open a fresh private/incognito browser window and sign in at https://10.50.0.1. In Live View, check that ADMIN_TO_FW_HTTPS allowed the new connection. An old browser tab could still be using an already-approved connection.

If the fresh connection fails, use the open VMware console to restore your saved configuration. Do not leave a broad allow-everything rule as the fix. Some releases have both legacy and new rule views; check both.

breakdown.meaning: A browser connection that already works may continue through a state. Test a fresh connection after the narrow rule and recovery path are ready.
An automatic management allow can take precedence over your rule. Preserve console recovery before removing it.

steps.expected: A fresh browser connection works through ADMIN_TO_FW_HTTPS. The broad LAN rules and automatic anti-lockout rule are disabled.

screenshot.title: Keep your administrator access working
screenshot.instructions: This original vendor image shows default LAN rules. Do not copy those broad allows into the final lab policy. Create and verify ADMIN_TO_FW_HTTPS first, then disable the broad LAN rules as written above.

steps.title: Allow only gateway-to-IIS web requests
steps.where: Windows host browser · Firewall → Rules → DMZ
actions: Open Firewall → Rules → DMZ. Click Add. Choose Pass, IPv4 and TCP.
Set Source to DMZ_PROXY and Destination to PRIVATE_IIS. Leave source port as any. Set destination port to HTTPS (443).
Check Log and enter description DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443. Save and apply. This permits the gateway to ask IIS for web pages only.
Add a second rule below it: Block, IPv4, any protocol, source DMZ net, destination any. Check Log and name it DMZ_DENY_OTHER. Save and apply.
Open the APP_PRIVATE rules tab. Add Block, IPv4, any protocol, source APP_PRIVATE net, destination any. Check Log and name it APP_DENY_OTHER. Save and apply.
Do not add general access to AD or SQL. Replies to an approved request use the firewall’s existing connection record, called a state; they do not need a broad reverse allow rule.
Keep the one DMZ web allow above the deny rule. Do not add source NAT between these internal networks. Export another private firewall backup.

breakdown.meaning: The proxy chooses a temporary client source port. Destination 443 is the HTTPS service we permit.
A reply to an approved request uses the existing state; it does not require allowing every new connection in the reverse direction.

steps.expected: DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443 sits above DMZ_DENY_OTHER. Other DMZ connections stay blocked; APP_PRIVATE also has its logged deny rule.

screenshot.title: Allow only gateway-to-IIS web requests
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443 is above DMZ_DENY_OTHER, and there is no broad DMZ-to-private allow.

lessons.title: Build the Private IIS Practice Website
lessons.description: Create a small test website on a new IIS server and let only the gateway reach it over HTTPS.
lessons.what: Create a small test website on a new IIS server and let only the gateway reach it over HTTPS.
lessons.why: We will start with a simple page that stands in for your help desk. This lets us prove the network works before adding an application and database. Your existing ticketing server stays untouched.
needs: Use only the fresh IIS-DMZ01 Server 2019 guest, not existing APP01. Install VMware Tools and keep the VM console available.
Download /dmz/new-iis-backend.ps1 on the Windows host if you prefer the complete script. Review it before running; the steps show the same operations.
bestPractices: Use the fresh dedicated IIS guest and keep its private key in the Windows certificate store.
commonMistakes: Leaving an older broad web allow enabled alongside the new scoped firewall rule.

troubleshooting.problem: The page does not load inside the server.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the DMZ-Lab site state, its C:\inetpub\dmz-lab path and loopback port 8080 first. Do not change network rules until the local health check succeeds.

lessons.pass: The site works locally, its HTTPS binding uses the expected name, the Windows firewall is scoped and only the public certificate is transferred.
lessons.exercise: Explain the difference between a contact hostname, a TLS certificate name, and an IP address.

quiz.question: What may be copied to the proxy?
options: The backend private key and Administrator password
quiz.explanation: The proxy needs public trust material to verify the backend; it does not need the backend private key.

steps.title: Set the private IIS server’s name and address
steps.where: IIS-DMZ01 guest console · Windows Server 2019 → ncpa.cpl
actions: Start the new IIS-DMZ01 VM. In VMware Settings, check that its only adapter is Custom VMnet5.
Sign in as the local Administrator. Open Server Manager → Local Server. Click Computer name → Change and enter IIS-DMZ01. Restart when asked.
Inside this Windows Server VM, press Windows+R, type ncpa.cpl and press Enter. Right-click Ethernet → Properties → Internet Protocol Version 4 → Properties.
Enter IP address 10.80.0.40, Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 and Default gateway 10.80.0.1. Leave DNS blank for this standalone practice server. Click OK twice.
Open Windows PowerShell as administrator inside IIS-DMZ01. Run ipconfig /all. Compare the IP, mask and gateway with your notebook.
Leave DC01 and DC02 alone. If 10.80.0.40 is already in use, stop and fix the address conflict before continuing.

breakdown.meaning: This fresh application VM does not need domain membership for the static HTTPS demonstration. That avoids opening AD service ports.

steps.expected: IIS-DMZ01 shows IP 10.80.0.40, mask 255.255.255.0 and gateway 10.80.0.1. Its only adapter is VMnet5; it is not a domain controller.

screenshot.title: Set the private IIS server’s name and address
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. IIS-DMZ01 is a workgroup VM at 10.80.0.40/24 with gateway 10.80.0.1 and exactly one VMnet5 NIC.

steps.title: Install IIS and open your test page
steps.where: IIS-DMZ01 · Windows PowerShell as Administrator
actions: In IIS-DMZ01’s administrator PowerShell, run hostname. It must print IIS-DMZ01. Do not paste the setup block into APP01 or your Windows host.
Copy the command block below and paste it into that PowerShell window. It installs IIS and creates a small page in C:\inetpub\dmz-lab.
This page stands in for your help desk. We are proving the protected web route before adding osTicket, PHP or a database.
The block stops Default Web Site on this new practice VM. It does not change your existing APP01 website.
Open IIS Manager → Sites. Look for DMZ-Lab. Its first test address is 127.0.0.1:8080, which works only from IIS-DMZ01 itself.
Run the local health check in the block. You should see the practice page. If it fails here, fix IIS before moving on to firewall or gateway testing.
steps.command:
if ($env:COMPUTERNAME -ne 'IIS-DMZ01') { throw 'Wrong VM. Stop here.' } Install-WindowsFeature Web-Server -IncludeManagementTools Import-Module WebAdministration New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path C:\inetpub\dmz-lab -Force '

CloudSeam DMZ lab

Private IIS backend: IIS-DMZ01

' | Set-Content C:\inetpub\dmz-lab\index.html Stop-Website 'Default Web Site' New-Website -Name 'DMZ-Lab' -PhysicalPath C:\inetpub\dmz-lab -IPAddress 127.0.0.1 -Port 8080 (Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:8080 -UseBasicParsing).StatusCode

breakdown.meaning: Adds the IIS server role and its management tools to this dedicated Windows guest.
127.0.0.1:8080 can be reached only inside this server; it lets you prove the page exists before testing the network.

steps.expected: The local test on IIS-DMZ01 returns your small practice webpage. DMZ-Lab appears in IIS Manager.

screenshot.title: Install IIS and open your test page
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The local health request returns the CloudSeam training page from the DMZ-Lab site.

steps.title: Add HTTPS to the private website
steps.where: IIS-DMZ01 · elevated PowerShell, then IIS Manager → DMZ-Lab → Bindings
actions: Stay in IIS-DMZ01’s administrator PowerShell. Run the command block below once. It creates a 30-day test certificate and adds HTTPS to DMZ-Lab.
A certificate helps the gateway check that it has reached the right website. Our private HTTPS name is iis-backend.cloudseam.tech.
Open IIS Manager → Sites → DMZ-Lab → Bindings. Check Type https, IP 10.80.0.40, Port 443 and Host name iis-backend.cloudseam.tech.
Check that SNI is enabled and the selected certificate is DMZ-Lab backend. SNI tells IIS which named HTTPS site the request wants.
Open C:\DMZ-Lab\backend-public.pem. It should have BEGIN CERTIFICATE and END CERTIFICATE lines. It must not contain PRIVATE KEY.
Keep the private key in Windows. Only copy the public PEM file later. This short-lived self-signed certificate is for our lab; real sites need managed trust and renewal.
steps.command:
$cert = New-SelfSignedCertificate -DnsName 'iis-backend.cloudseam.tech' -CertStoreLocation 'Cert:\LocalMachine\My' -FriendlyName 'DMZ-Lab backend' -KeyAlgorithm RSA -KeyLength 3072 -HashAlgorithm SHA256 -NotAfter (Get-Date).AddDays(30)
New-WebBinding -Name 'DMZ-Lab' -Protocol https -IPAddress '10.80.0.40' -Port 443 -HostHeader 'iis-backend.cloudseam.tech' -SslFlags 1
(Get-WebBinding -Name 'DMZ-Lab' -Protocol https).AddSslCertificate($cert.Thumbprint, 'My')
New-Item -ItemType Directory C:\DMZ-Lab -Force
$pem = '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----' + "`r`n" + [Convert]::ToBase64String($cert.RawData, [System.Base64FormattingOptions]::InsertLineBreaks) + "`r`n-----END CERTIFICATE-----`r`n"
$pem | Set-Content C:\DMZ-Lab\backend-public.pem -Encoding Ascii

breakdown.meaning: Adds the expected backend name to the test certificate.
Enables SNI so IIS selects the HTTPS binding by the hostname sent during TLS.
A text-encoded certificate used for verification. It must not include the server’s private key.

steps.expected: IIS has the HTTPS binding for iis-backend.cloudseam.tech. backend-public.pem contains the public certificate, with no private key.

screenshot.title: Add HTTPS to the private website
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The correct SNI HTTPS binding exists, and backend-public.pem contains only the backend’s public certificate.

steps.title: Limit IIS access and copy its public certificate
steps.where: IIS-DMZ01 · elevated PowerShell; Windows host → Workstation shared folder settings
actions: On IIS-DMZ01, run the firewall command below. It allows HTTPS from PROXY01 at 10.60.0.10.

Open Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security → Inbound Rules. Review enabled Allow rules for TCP 80 and 443. Disable broad web rules on this dedicated practice VM that would also allow other computers through.
Keep Windows Firewall on. A narrow new rule does not cancel an older allow-everyone rule.
On your Windows host, create the folder C:\DMZ-Transfer. In IIS-DMZ01 VMware Settings → Options → Shared Folders, temporarily add it with share name DMZ-Transfer.
Inside IIS-DMZ01, copy C:\DMZ-Lab\backend-public.pem to \\vmware-host\Shared Folders\DMZ-Transfer. Check that you copied only the public certificate, not a password, PFX or private key.
We will turn off this shared folder after copying the public files to the Linux VMs. It is a temporary file transfer, not the network route our visitors will use.
steps.command:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'DMZ-Lab HTTPS from proxy only' -Direction Inbound -Action Allow -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 443 -RemoteAddress 10.60.0.10 -Profile Any
Get-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'DMZ-Lab HTTPS from proxy only' | Get-NetFirewallAddressFilter
# Inspect other inbound web allows on this dedicated VM before disabling them.
Get-NetFirewallRule -Direction Inbound -Enabled True -Action Allow | Where-Object DisplayName -Match 'World Wide Web|HTTPS|HTTP' | Select-Object Name,DisplayName,Enabled

breakdown.meaning: Limits the inbound allow to the proxy. Other enabled broad allow rules must be reviewed too; adding a narrow allow does not override them.

steps.expected: Only the gateway IP is allowed through the Windows HTTPS rule. The shared folder contains only the public certificate file.

screenshot.title: Limit IIS access and copy its public certificate
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The Windows HTTPS rule is scoped to 10.60.0.10, and only the public backend PEM is staged for the proxy.

lessons.title: Build the Gateway in the DMZ
lessons.description: Set up NGINX on AlmaLinux so it can accept visitor requests and forward them to private IIS.
lessons.what: Set up NGINX on AlmaLinux so it can accept visitor requests and forward them to private IIS.
lessons.why: NGINX is our reverse proxy, or web gateway. It receives a request, asks IIS for the page and returns the answer. The visitor never receives general access to the private network.
needs: PROXY01 has its packages installed from the preparation stage and one VMnet3 NIC.
The public backend PEM is in the temporary host folder. Use the dedicated VM console; public SSH is not needed.
bestPractices: Verify the private TLS hop before debugging the complete visitor route.
commonMistakes: Treating an HTTPS upstream URL as proof that the upstream certificate is being checked.

troubleshooting.problem: NGINX starts but the backend request fails.
troubleshooting.fix: Run the direct --cacert/--resolve backend test from PROXY01. Match the firewall decision, certificate SAN, clock and IIS binding before changing the proxy.

lessons.pass: The direct verified backend test succeeds and the proxy service starts with certificate checks and host protections enabled.
lessons.exercise: Read the downloaded configuration and identify which lines control the visitor hostname, backend hostname, upstream IP, and trust certificate.

quiz.question: Which setting protects the proxy-to-backend HTTPS connection?
options: proxy_ssl_verify on with the expected backend name and trust certificate
quiz.explanation: Encryption and certificate/hostname verification are both required; an HTTPS URL alone does not guarantee verification.

steps.title: Set the gateway’s DMZ address
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console
actions: Open PROXY01’s VMware console and sign in. Run nmcli connection show. Find the one Ethernet connection; ignore loopback. Write its exact name in your notes.
In the command block below, replace the example connection name with that exact name. Keep the quotes around a name that contains spaces.
Run the block to set address 10.60.0.10/24 and gateway 10.60.0.1. DNS is empty because this practice uses explicit addresses and certificate names.
Check the output from ip -4 address and ip -4 route. You should see the DMZ address and one default route through 10.60.0.1.
If you still see a VMnet8/NAT address, shut down PROXY01 and fix its VMware adapter before continuing.
Run timedatectl. Check the date and time. A badly wrong clock can make a valid certificate appear expired.
steps.command:
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname proxy01.cloudseam.tech
nmcli connection show
# Replace YOUR_CONNECTION with the exact Ethernet profile name above.
sudo nmcli connection modify "YOUR_CONNECTION" ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.60.0.10/24 ipv4.gateway 10.60.0.1 ipv4.dns "" ipv6.method disabled
sudo nmcli connection up "YOUR_CONNECTION"
ip -4 address
ip -4 route
timedatectl

breakdown.meaning: nmcli modifies the named Ethernet profile. The profile name can contain spaces, so keep the quotes.
10.60.0.1 is the firewall doorway for destinations outside PROXY01’s own subnet.

steps.expected: PROXY01 shows 10.60.0.10/24 and default gateway 10.60.0.1. No temporary NAT adapter remains.

screenshot.title: Set the gateway’s DMZ address
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. PROXY01 has only 10.60.0.10/24 on its Ethernet NIC and uses 10.60.0.1 as gateway.

steps.title: Test the gateway’s connection to IIS
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console; Workstation Options → Shared Folders
actions: On the host, open PROXY01 VMware Settings → Options → Shared Folders. Temporarily add C:\DMZ-Transfer with share name DMZ-Transfer.
In PROXY01’s console, run the mount and copy block below. It copies backend-public.pem, the public certificate from IIS. Do not copy a private key.

Run the curl test in the block. curl requests a web page from the terminal. --resolve sends it to 10.80.0.40 using the correct website name; --cacert checks the certificate against the public file you copied.
Look for the practice page from IIS. Do not add -k to hide a certificate error.
On FW01, open Firewall → Log Files → Live View. Find a Pass for source 10.60.0.10 and rule DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443.
If the request fails, check the address, rule, IIS binding, certificate name and clock. Get this direct gateway-to-IIS test working before adding the gateway service.
steps.command:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/dmz-transfer
sudo vmhgfs-fuse .host:/DMZ-Transfer /mnt/dmz-transfer -o allow_other
sudo cp /mnt/dmz-transfer/backend-public.pem /etc/pki/tls/certs/iis-backend.pem
curl --cacert /etc/pki/tls/certs/iis-backend.pem --resolve iis-backend.cloudseam.tech:443:10.80.0.40 --connect-timeout 5 https://iis-backend.cloudseam.tech/

breakdown.meaning: Tells curl which specific public certificate to trust for this lab connection.
Connects to the private IP while retaining the correct URL hostname for TLS and IIS SNI.

steps.expected: The gateway receives the IIS practice page with the certificate check enabled. FW01 logs the matching allowed request.

screenshot.title: Test the gateway’s connection to IIS
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. A verified curl request from PROXY01 reaches the private IIS page and a matching narrow firewall pass is logged.

steps.title: Create the gateway’s test certificate
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console
actions: Stay on PROXY01. Run the OpenSSL block below to make a second, 30-day test certificate. This one belongs to app-dmz.cloudseam.tech, the name visitors use.
The command sets the private key to permission 600. That means only its owner, root, can read or change it.
Run the inspection command in the block. Check the certificate name and dates. SAN lists the names that the certificate covers; it must include app-dmz.cloudseam.tech.
Copy only dmz-front.crt into the shared folder, with filename proxy-public.crt. TEST01 needs this public file to check the gateway’s identity.
Never copy dmz-front.key. A real public website would use a trusted certificate service and renewal, not this temporary test certificate.
steps.command:
sudo openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:3072 -sha256 -days 30 -keyout /etc/pki/tls/private/dmz-front.key -out /etc/pki/tls/certs/dmz-front.crt -subj "/CN=app-dmz.cloudseam.tech" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:app-dmz.cloudseam.tech"
sudo chmod 600 /etc/pki/tls/private/dmz-front.key
openssl x509 -in /etc/pki/tls/certs/dmz-front.crt -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName
sudo cp /etc/pki/tls/certs/dmz-front.crt /mnt/dmz-transfer/proxy-public.crt

breakdown.meaning: The certificate name must match app-dmz.cloudseam.tech, the name the visitor requests.
The secret file stays on the proxy with restrictive permissions. Only the public certificate goes to TEST01.

steps.expected: The gateway certificate covers app-dmz.cloudseam.tech and has the expected dates. Only root can read its private key.

screenshot.title: Create the gateway’s test certificate
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The front certificate has the correct SAN and dates; the front private key stays root-only on PROXY01.

steps.title: Copy and check the NGINX configuration
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console / text editor
actions: On the Windows host, click NGINX configuration in this step’s downloads. Save nginx-dmz.conf in C:\DMZ-Transfer.
Open the file and read it first. It sends requests to private IIS at 10.80.0.40:443. It does not point at APP01.
On PROXY01, run the copy command below. It places the file at /etc/nginx/conf.d/dmz.conf. The gateway listens at 10.60.0.10:443 for app-dmz.cloudseam.tech.

Keep proxy_ssl_verify on. Keep proxy_ssl_name set to iis-backend.cloudseam.tech and keep the backend PEM trust file. These settings check the private IIS certificate instead of blindly trusting any server.
The file replaces X-Forwarded-For with the visitor’s actual connection address. That header carries a client address; it is not proof that a user is signed in.
Run nginx -t. Look for a successful configuration test. Fix any reported file path, certificate or syntax error before starting NGINX.

breakdown.meaning: Makes NGINX verify the backend certificate instead of merely encrypting to an unchecked endpoint.
The verified TLS name is iis-backend.cloudseam.tech even though the connection uses the IP 10.80.0.40.
IIS uses its backend host binding. The visitor-facing hostname does not have to be the backend binding name.

steps.expected: nginx -t reports that the configuration test succeeded. The settings still verify the private IIS certificate.

screenshot.title: Copy and check the NGINX configuration
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. nginx -t reports a valid configuration with upstream certificate verification enabled.

steps.title: Start NGINX and keep protections on
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console
actions: On PROXY01, run the SELinux command below. It lets the web service make an outgoing connection to IIS. SELinux stays on; the firewall still limits where that connection may go.
Run firewall-cmd --get-active-zones. Find the zone containing your Ethernet interface. The block below uses public; if yours differs, use that zone name consistently.
Add the HTTPS rule in the block. It accepts requests from TEST01 at 10.70.0.10 only.
Review the zone’s services. Remove any broad http or https allowance on this dedicated VM that would also let other sources in. Do not stop firewalld.
Run the service start and check commands. NGINX should be active and listening on 10.60.0.10:443.
Leave the shared folder only until TEST01 copies its public certificate in the next lesson. Then unmount it and disable Shared Folders on the practice VMs.
steps.command:
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.70.0.10/32" service name="https" accept'
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
systemctl is-active nginx
getenforce
sudo ss -lntp | grep ':443'

breakdown.meaning: Allows the web-service process to make an upstream connection while SELinux remains enforcing.
The visitor HTTPS rule names TEST01. FW01 independently limits which private endpoint the proxy may reach.

steps.expected: NGINX is active at 10.60.0.10:443. SELinux and firewalld remain on, with HTTPS allowed only from TEST01.

screenshot.title: Start NGINX and keep protections on
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. SELinux is enforcing, firewalld has the scoped visitor HTTPS rule, and NGINX is active on the DMZ listener.

lessons.title: Open the Practice Help Desk as a Visitor
lessons.description: Give TEST01 its address, open one HTTPS doorway and request the page through the gateway.
lessons.what: Give TEST01 its address, open one HTTPS doorway and request the page through the gateway.
lessons.why: We have built the pieces separately. Now we will connect them. TEST01 pretends to be an outside visitor, but everything still stays inside VMware. No home-router or public DNS changes are needed.
needs: The private IIS hop and proxy configuration already pass their local checks.
TEST01 has curl, OpenSSL and open-vm-tools installed; its only NIC is VMnet4.
bestPractices: Publish only the one intended HTTPS listener and test from the single-NIC visitor.
commonMistakes: Testing from the administrator host, which already has private-network access.

troubleshooting.problem: My interface names or addresses differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and compare the MAC address and VMnet assignment on each adapter. Use the VMware console to recover access; do not guess which interface is private.

lessons.pass: A real TEST01 request, firewall records and proxy log entry all show the intended visitor-to-proxy-to-private-IIS route.
lessons.exercise: Trace both TLS connections and explain which server presents each certificate.

quiz.question: Why use --resolve in this local exercise?
options: To publish the lab in Cloudflare
To use the correct hostname/TLS name while connecting to the isolated outside IP
quiz.explanation: The request uses the intended hostname without changing public DNS; --cacert still verifies the certificate.

steps.title: Set the practice visitor’s address
steps.where: TEST01 · AlmaLinux 9 GNOME Settings → Network
actions: Start TEST01. In AlmaLinux GNOME, open Settings → Network → the gear beside Wired → IPv4. Select Manual.
Enter Address 10.70.0.10, Netmask 255.255.255.0 and Gateway 10.70.0.1.
Turn off automatic DNS and leave DNS empty. Click Apply. Switch Wired off, then on to reconnect.
Open Terminal and run ip -4 route. The default gateway should be 10.70.0.1, not a VMware NAT address.
Check VMware Settings: TEST01 must have just one adapter, Custom VMnet4. It should have no private or DMZ adapter.
Use TEST01 for visitor tests. It acts like an outside user while staying inside this isolated lab.
steps.command:
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname test01.cloudseam.tech
ip -4 address
ip -4 route

breakdown.meaning: TEST01 sits on VMnet4 only. The host’s management adapter is not an outside test machine.

steps.expected: TEST01 shows 10.70.0.10/24 and gateway 10.70.0.1. Its only VMware adapter is VMnet4.

screenshot.title: Set the practice visitor’s address
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. TEST01 is 10.70.0.10/24 with one VMnet4 NIC and gateway 10.70.0.1.

steps.title: Send visitor HTTPS requests to the gateway
steps.where: Windows host browser · FW01 → Firewall → NAT → Destination NAT / Port Forward
actions: In FW01’s web interface, open Firewall → NAT → Port Forward. Click Add. Select WAN/OUTSIDE, IPv4 and TCP.
Set Source to LAB_VISITOR. Leave source port as any. Set Destination to WAN address and destination port to HTTPS (443).
Set Redirect target IP to DMZ_PROXY (10.60.0.10) and Redirect target port to 443. Enter description OUTSIDE_HTTPS_TO_PROXY.

Choose the associated filter-rule option to create its matching outside allow rule. If your release requires a separate filter rule, follow that release’s documentation and keep the same narrow visitor and HTTPS limits. Save and apply.
Open the OUTSIDE rules tab. Check that the resulting Pass allows only LAB_VISITOR to the translated gateway HTTPS service.
Below it, add a logged Block rule: IPv4, any protocol, source LAB_VISITOR, destination any. Name it OUTSIDE_DENY_OTHER. Save and apply.
Do not forward visitors directly to IIS at 10.80.0.40. Do not publish RDP, SQL or firewall administration. Leave reflection/hairpin off and do not add source NAT between the internal networks.

breakdown.meaning: Rewrites the outside HTTPS destination to the proxy’s DMZ address. The accompanying firewall rule still needs to allow that specific flow.
The private IIS connection should retain PROXY01’s 10.60.0.10 source, which its Windows firewall expects.

steps.expected: One HTTPS forwarding rule sends the practice visitor to PROXY01. There is no direct outside forward to IIS.

screenshot.title: Send visitor HTTPS requests to the gateway
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. One outside TCP 443 forward points to PROXY01, with its narrow pass rule; IIS has no outside forward.

steps.title: Copy the certificate the visitor needs
steps.where: TEST01 · AlmaLinux Terminal; temporary VMware shared folder
actions: In TEST01 VMware Settings → Options → Shared Folders, temporarily add C:\DMZ-Transfer with share name DMZ-Transfer.
In TEST01 Terminal, run the copy block below. It copies proxy-public.crt into your home folder. This is the gateway’s public certificate, not its private key.

Run the fingerprint command. On PROXY01, run the same command against /etc/pki/tls/certs/dmz-front.crt. Compare every part of the SHA-256 fingerprint. Matching fingerprints mean you have the same certificate file.
Do not copy a .key file or a backend private key. Do not add an unknown root certificate to your everyday computer.
Unmount the share on TEST01 and PROXY01. Disable Shared Folders in the VMware settings of TEST01, PROXY01 and IIS-DMZ01.
Keep these public files in your own lab folder. Do not upload certificate keys or firewall backups to your academy notebook.
steps.command:
mkdir -p ~/dmz-lab
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/dmz-transfer
sudo vmhgfs-fuse .host:/DMZ-Transfer /mnt/dmz-transfer -o allow_other
cp /mnt/dmz-transfer/proxy-public.crt ~/dmz-lab/
openssl x509 -in ~/dmz-lab/proxy-public.crt -noout -fingerprint -sha256
sudo umount /mnt/dmz-transfer

breakdown.meaning: Compare the complete SHA-256 fingerprint on both machines to confirm you transferred the intended public certificate.

steps.expected: TEST01 has the gateway’s matching public certificate. Shared Folders is now disabled on all practice VMs.

screenshot.title: Copy the certificate the visitor needs
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. TEST01 has the matching front public certificate and all temporary shared folders are disabled.

steps.title: Open the page through the full route
steps.where: TEST01 · AlmaLinux Terminal
actions: In TEST01 Terminal, run the curl command below. It asks for app-dmz.cloudseam.tech through FW01’s outside address, 10.70.0.1.
--resolve supplies a local address for this one request, so no public DNS change is needed. --cacert checks the gateway against the public certificate you copied.
Look for the CloudSeam DMZ practice page. Do not add -k if the certificate check fails.
On FW01, open Live View and find the outside allow followed by the DMZ-to-IIS allow. On PROXY01, check the access log for TEST01’s address and request path.
Save the request time and what you actually saw in My lab notebook. The illustrated output is an example, not proof that your own test worked.
The example page identifies the backend to help you learn. Real public pages should not reveal internal server names.

breakdown.meaning: TEST01 verifies the front certificate; NGINX separately verifies the IIS backend certificate.
A harmless query value that helps match this request in logs. It is not a password or an authentication token.

steps.expected: TEST01 receives the private IIS practice page through PROXY01, with certificate checking enabled.

screenshot.title: Open the page through the full route
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The request succeeds with TLS verification and returns the page created on private IIS through PROXY01.

lessons.title: Check What Visitors Can and Cannot Reach
lessons.description: Prove that the website works through the gateway while direct access to private services stays blocked.
lessons.what: Prove that the website works through the gateway while direct access to private services stays blocked.
lessons.why: A working page is only half the test. We also need to show that unwanted connections fail for the right reason. A matching firewall log tells us which rule blocked the request.
needs: Keep the successful end-to-end request and direct backend test as baselines.
Only test the approved practice IPs and named ports. Do not scan public addresses or unrelated machines.
bestPractices: Keep a positive baseline and correlate each failed test with its actual firewall decision.
commonMistakes: Calling every timeout a security success without finding why the connection failed.

troubleshooting.problem: My interface names or addresses differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and compare the MAC address and VMnet assignment on each adapter. Use the VMware console to recover access; do not guess which interface is private.

lessons.pass: The saved matrix includes successful published HTTPS plus logged blocks for direct outside access and DMZ management/domain attempts.
lessons.exercise: Teach someone why a stateful firewall permits the HTTPS response without allowing the backend to initiate arbitrary DMZ connections.

quiz.question: Does a timeout alone prove the firewall blocked a connection?
options: No; correlate the firewall decision and a known-working service
quiz.explanation: A missing route, stopped listener and firewall block can look similar from the client. Correlated evidence avoids guessing.

steps.title: Check that visitors cannot reach IIS directly
steps.where: TEST01 · AlmaLinux Terminal; FW01 Live View
actions: On TEST01, run the TCP connection check below. It tries to reach private IIS directly at 10.80.0.40:443, skipping the gateway.
This attempt should fail or time out. A timeout alone does not tell us why, so check the firewall next.
On FW01, open Firewall → Log Files → Live View. Filter Source to 10.70.0.10 and Destination to 10.80.0.40. Find a Block from OUTSIDE_DENY_OTHER at the time of your test.
Repeat the approved gateway curl request from the previous lesson. It should still return the page. Record both results in My lab notebook.
If direct access succeeds, disable the outside publishing rule while you investigate. Look for a broad allow, an old connection state or an extra VMware adapter. Fix the bypass before continuing.
steps.command:
timeout 5 bash -c '</dev/tcp/10.80.0.40/443'
echo "TCP probe exit status: $?"

breakdown.meaning: The /dev/tcp check tests whether a connection can open. A timeout or rejection still needs a matching firewall decision to explain it.

steps.expected: Direct visitor access to IIS fails with a matching firewall Block. The approved gateway request still works.

screenshot.title: Check that visitors cannot reach IIS directly
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. Direct outside TCP 443 to the private IIS address is blocked with a matching firewall record, while the approved proxy request still succeeds.

steps.title: Check that private management stays blocked
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console; FW01 Live View
actions: On PROXY01, run the two TCP checks below. One tries the IIS remote-desktop port; the other tries DC01’s file-sharing port. Both should be blocked.
In FW01 Live View, find a matching DMZ_DENY_OTHER Block for each attempt from 10.60.0.10. Do not change DC01’s services to force a failure.
If you already have SQL01, use its recorded lab address for one additional check on TCP 1433. Do not guess an address. A stopped SQL service alone does not prove a firewall block.
Repeat the verified backend curl test from PROXY01. The approved web connection to 10.80.0.40:443 should still work.
On IIS-DMZ01, open administrator PowerShell. Run Test-NetConnection 10.50.0.10 -Port 445. Check that TcpTestSucceeded is False and find the matching APP_DENY_OTHER Block on FW01.
Save the results and matching rule names. Our application network must not have general access to AD or SQL.

breakdown.meaning: An intentional attempt that should be blocked. Test only your named practice addresses and confirm the rule that denied it.
IIS is on VMnet5, separate from AD. Its attempt to reach DC01 must cross FW01 and meet APP_DENY_OTHER.

steps.expected: The management checks fail with matching Block logs. Gateway-to-IIS HTTPS still works. IIS-to-AD access is also blocked.

screenshot.title: Check that private management stays blocked
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The DMZ can reach only the intended private HTTPS service; the tested RDP/SMB paths have matching deny logs.

steps.title: Save the test results and check the adapters
steps.where: Windows host browser · FW01 Live View and Workstation settings
actions: On FW01, open Firewall → Log Files → Live View. For each test, filter by its source and destination. Record the time, interface, rule name and Pass or Block result.
Download Traffic test checklist below. Fill in your observed results; the planned result is not evidence until you test it.
In VMware Settings, check FW01’s four custom adapters. Check that PROXY01, IIS-DMZ01 and TEST01 each have only one.
Confirm temporary Shared Folders are off and no NAT or bridged bypass adapter remains.
Check that firewall administration still works from your Windows host’s private management adapter. Do not use that host as your outside visitor test.
Remember why VMnet5 matters: IIS traffic to AD must cross the firewall. Servers sharing VMnet2 can talk directly to one another, so placing IIS there would not prove this separation.
Save your completed results in My lab notebook. A VMnet is a virtual switch; it does not replace firewall rules.

breakdown.meaning: Devices on the same virtual switch can communicate without traversing a router. Separate application and AD networks make the firewall boundary meaningful.

steps.expected: Your saved checklist has both working and blocked tests, each matched to a log. No extra adapter or shared folder bypass remains.

screenshot.title: Save the test results and check the adapters
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The connection matrix has both allowed and denied evidence, and the inventory shows no alternate route around FW01.

lessons.title: Find a Problem and Get the Website Working Again
lessons.description: Follow a request through the logs, break one practice rule, and restore the working setup.
lessons.what: Follow a request through the logs, break one practice rule, and restore the working setup.
lessons.why: Troubleshooting is easier when you follow the same path as the request. We will check one part at a time, keep a backup and undo one controlled change.
needs: The complete allowed/blocked matrix passes before you introduce a fault.
Save FW01 configuration privately, copy the NGINX configuration locally and keep all VM consoles available.
bestPractices: Change one thing at a time, record a baseline and retest allowed and blocked paths after rollback.
commonMistakes: Opening extra ports or disabling certificate verification to hide an unresolved upstream error.

troubleshooting.problem: My interface names or addresses differ.
troubleshooting.fix: Stop and compare the MAC address and VMnet assignment on each adapter. Use the VMware console to recover access; do not guess which interface is private.

lessons.pass: You have recovered one deliberate rule failure and recorded a repeatable rollback with passing positive and negative tests.
lessons.exercise: Given a 502 response, list the checks in the order you would use and explain what each result rules out.

quiz.question: What is the safest response to an upstream certificate-name error?
options: Correct the expected name, certificate SAN and trust configuration
quiz.explanation: Repair the identity/trust mismatch and retest the secure path. Disabling verification hides the problem.

steps.title: Find the same request in both logs
steps.where: PROXY01 terminal; IIS-DMZ01 → IIS Manager → DMZ-Lab → Logging
actions: On TEST01, request the page again with a unique labtrace value in the URL, as shown below. Write down the time. Check that the server clocks roughly agree.

On PROXY01, read /var/log/nginx/dmz-access.log and /var/log/nginx/dmz-error.log. Find the request using its labtrace, visitor IP, response code and upstream status. Upstream means the IIS server behind the gateway.
On IIS-DMZ01, open IIS Manager → DMZ-Lab → Logging. Note the log folder and site ID. Open the newest W3SVC log there.
The IIS client address, c-ip, should be 10.60.0.10 because IIS receives the gateway’s connection.

To also record the original visitor, choose Select Fields → Add Field. Name it ClientIP, choose Request Header and enter X-Forwarded-For. Trust this field only from the approved gateway, which replaces visitor-supplied values.
Write the matching time and result in your notebook. Do not paste passwords, tokens or real customer records.

breakdown.meaning: IIS sees the proxy as its TCP peer. A forwarded client field is useful only when accepted from your trusted proxy.
Match a time and request identifier across the client, firewall, proxy and IIS rather than guessing from one screen.

steps.expected: You find the same labtrace request in the gateway and IIS logs. IIS sees the gateway as its connecting client.

screenshot.title: Find the same request in both logs
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The same labtrace request can be matched across proxy and IIS logs with the expected proxy/client distinction.

steps.title: Break and restore one firewall rule
steps.where: Windows host browser · FW01 DMZ rule list; TEST01 terminal
actions: First send a successful TEST01 request and note the time. Export a private firewall backup. Keep the VMware firewall console open.
In FW01 → Firewall → Rules → DMZ, disable only DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443. Keep DMZ_DENY_OTHER enabled. Apply.
Open Firewall → Diagnostics → States. Clear only states matching 10.60.0.10 → 10.80.0.40:443. An already-approved connection might otherwise keep working.
From TEST01, request the same page. Wait for the configured timeout. Read the actual error; do not assume a particular response code.
On PROXY01, check the NGINX error log. On FW01, find the matching Block. This shows the gateway cannot reach IIS; it is not a reason to open every port.
Re-enable DMZ_PROXY_TO_IIS_443 and apply. Send a fresh request. Repeat your blocked-path tests too. Save what failed and what fixed it.

breakdown.meaning: Disabling an allow may not remove connections already admitted. Clear only the matching test states, not every management session.

steps.expected: The request fails when the one rule is disabled. It works again after that rule is restored, and your blocked-path tests still fail.

screenshot.title: Break and restore one firewall rule
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. A deliberately blocked upstream is diagnosed from logs and recovered by restoring the single known rule.

steps.title: Tell certificate and network problems apart
steps.where: PROXY01 · AlmaLinux console
actions: On PROXY01, run nginx -t and systemctl status nginx. Then run the verified direct backend curl test. Read the exact error before changing anything.

If the certificate is expired, check the clock first. If it really expired, renew the lab certificate and verify the replacement public file before updating the trust file. Keep the old configuration and certificate backed up.
If the error says the name does not match, compare proxy_ssl_name in NGINX, the certificate SAN and the IIS SNI binding. All must use iis-backend.cloudseam.tech.
If the error says permission denied, check the SELinux setting and audit log. Leave SELinux enforcing. If the request times out, check the firewall rule and whether IIS is listening.
After your fix, run nginx -t before reloading NGINX. Repeat the allowed and blocked tests. Do not turn off certificate verification as a shortcut.
steps.command:
sudo nginx -t
systemctl status nginx --no-pager
getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
openssl x509 -in /etc/pki/tls/certs/iis-backend.pem -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName
sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/nginx/dmz-error.log

breakdown.meaning: A wrong name, expired certificate or wrong public trust file is a different problem from a blocked network path. Fix the reported cause.

steps.expected: You can use the error message to choose the right check: configuration, certificate, clock, service permission or firewall.

screenshot.title: Tell certificate and network problems apart
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. You can identify whether the fault is configuration, name/trust, time, service policy or a blocked network path.

steps.title: Practice restoring a working backup
steps.where: Windows host · Workstation consoles and private change notes
actions: Before a patch or large change, shut down the dedicated FW01, PROXY01 and IIS-DMZ01 VMs. In VMware, take a snapshot of each. Give it a date and a clear reason, such as before-proxy-update.
Write the snapshot names and private backup locations in your notebook. Do not take or restore DC01/DC02 snapshots for this exercise. A snapshot is not a replacement for a tested backup.
If a change breaks the lab, disable the outside NAT rule first so new visitor requests stop.
Use the VMware console to restore the last working firewall backup, configuration file or dedicated VM snapshot, as appropriate.
Check the adapter mappings, certificate trust files and HTTPS rule after restoring. Repeat both the working-page test and the blocked-path tests.
Only re-enable the outside NAT rule after those checks pass. Write what failed, what you restored and which tests passed so another person could follow your recovery.

breakdown.meaning: A short-lived VM checkpoint helps a lab rollback. A separate, tested backup is still needed for recovery from lost or damaged VM files.

steps.expected: Your notes identify the working backup, restore order and test results. DC01 and DC02 were not restored or changed.

screenshot.title: Practice restoring a working backup
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. Your recovery notes identify the exact checkpoint, restore order and full validation matrix without touching AD.

lessons.title: Plan the Azure Version and Close the Lab
lessons.description: Compare the same design with Azure, estimate the costs and shut down the local practice machines.
lessons.what: Compare the same design with Azure, estimate the costs and shut down the local practice machines.
lessons.why: The same idea works in Azure: a public web doorway in front of a private application. The services and bills are different, so this lesson is a plan. It does not create paid Azure resources.
needs: Finish the on-premises traffic and recovery tests.
This lesson is planning only. It does not ask you to deploy Azure resources or alter the live cloudseam.tech website.
bestPractices: Cost the whole architecture and define cleanup before approving a cloud deployment.
commonMistakes: Assuming that stopping one VM or adding a tag stops every Azure charge.

troubleshooting.problem: The gateway estimate exceeds the practice budget.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the exercise local and save the Azure diagram/cost comparison. Do not create a paid gateway to finish this planning lesson.

lessons.pass: A costed Azure design comparison and a clean local shutdown/handover are complete; no paid cloud resources were created.
lessons.exercise: Explain the design to a manager: why local practice is the starting point, what changes in Azure and which costs remain after stopping a VM.

quiz.question: Does deallocating an Azure VM stop every charge in the architecture?
options: No; disks, IPs, gateways and other resources may continue billing
Only if the VM has a tag
quiz.explanation: Cost management needs a resource-by-resource cleanup plan. Tags help identify ownership and expiry; they do not stop billing by themselves.

steps.title: Draw the same design in Azure
steps.where: Your notebook · Azure architecture planning
actions: Draw an Azure version of the same route: visitor → Application Gateway WAF v2 → private IIS VM. WAF means web application firewall; it can inspect web requests for common attacks.
Give Application Gateway its own dedicated subnet. Put IIS in a separate private subnet with no public IP on the VM.

Plan to allow backend HTTPS only from the approved gateway and approved administration path. Use Azure Network Security Groups, or NSGs, plus the Windows firewall. Do not allow all Internet traffic to IIS.
Keep AD and databases private. Add only the application and management connections they really require; plan private DNS and private endpoints where needed.

Choose an Azure address range that does not overlap your local lab. Plan VPN or ExpressRoute and DNS separately if connecting the two environments. VMware host-only networks do not automatically exist in Azure.
Use the existing Azure migration and maintenance classes for an actual move or Windows upgrade. This diagram does not migrate or deploy anything.

breakdown.meaning: The security goal carries over; VMware adapter names and host-only settings do not.
The application has no VM public IP. Its inbound web traffic is restricted to the approved ingress service.

steps.expected: Your Azure drawing puts the public gateway and private IIS in separate subnets. The IIS VM has no public IP.

screenshot.title: Draw the same design in Azure
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The Azure diagram separates managed ingress, private application and data/domain tiers, with no public IP on the backend VM.

steps.title: Estimate Azure costs before building
steps.where: Windows host browser · Azure pricing calculator and your budget notes
actions: Open the Azure pricing calculator. Select your intended region. Add Application Gateway/WAF, VM compute, disks, public IP, backup, logs and outgoing network traffic.
Write the estimated cost, region, date and running hours in My lab notebook. This is an estimate, not a spending limit.
Compare with using your existing local hardware. OPNsense Community, AlmaLinux and NGINX have no subscription fee for this exercise. Windows evaluation terms, electricity and hardware still matter.
Do not expect this always-on managed gateway design to fit a $25 monthly budget. A small temporary proxy VM is a different design with different protections and availability.

For any later Azure build, set an end time and a deletion checklist before starting. Stopping a VM does not remove disk, public IP or gateway charges. Budget alerts warn you; they do not automatically cap the bill.
Do not click Create during this lesson. Leave the academy website and public DNS unchanged.

breakdown.meaning: Disks, public IPs and gateways can continue billing after a VM is stopped. Estimate each resource.
Tags identify the owner and expiry for reports or automation. A tag by itself does not stop a resource or reduce its rate.

steps.expected: Your notes include the region, running hours, estimated charges and deletion plan. No Azure resources were created.

screenshot.title: Estimate Azure costs before building
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. Your comparison includes fixed and running costs, a runtime/deletion plan and no deployed Azure resources.

steps.title: Save your work and shut down the lab
steps.where: Windows host · Workstation Pro and lab notebook
actions: Click Save notes, then Download my notes. Keep your diagram, adapter MACs, rule checklist and test times. Keep private firewall backups outside public repositories.
If leaving any VMs running, disable the outside NAT rule. Otherwise shut down TEST01, PROXY01, IIS-DMZ01 and FW01 cleanly.
Check that temporary Shared Folders are off and installer ISOs are disconnected. Confirm you did not create a home-router forward, public DNS record, bridge or tunnel.
Keep the VM files if you want to practice again. Remove old dedicated-lab snapshots only after checking your backup. Do not delete DC01, DC02, APP01 or the VMnet2 network used by other classes.

Before a real public launch, plan supported updates, trusted certificates and renewal, monitoring, backups, access control, availability and a WAF where appropriate. This practice lab teaches the pattern; it does not certify a production deployment.

breakdown.meaning: A second administrator should be able to rebuild and verify the design from your diagram, configuration inventory and traffic-test matrix.

steps.expected: The four practice VMs are shut down. Your notes and private backups are saved, ready for another practice session.

screenshot.title: Save your work and shut down the lab
screenshot.instructions: Use the numbered controls as a guide, then compare the result on your own lab machine. The four dedicated VMs are stopped, no real Internet exposure exists, and another learner can follow the saved runbook.
